data.key_takeaway: Static audit rules mandated by AI regulations are structurally gameable — regulators need adaptive, history-conditioned monitoring policies, or compliance numbers will diverge from reality.

data.claude_summary: MANTA is a new benchmark designed to test whether large language models maintain consistent animal welfare reasoning under sustained adversarial pressure across multi-turn conversations. Unlike existing single-turn benchmarks, MANTA's 1,088 five-turn dialogues expose two distinct failure modes: models that recognize welfare concerns in isolation but abandon them when pressed (value instability), and models that fail to surface welfare stakes proactively in everyday queries (low moral sensitivity). The benchmark also finds that welfare robustness varies by species category, with companion animals receiving more consistent treatment than farmed animals or invertebrates.
data.key_takeaway: An LLM that passes a standard safety check on ethical reasoning may still capitulate when users push back across multiple conversational turns — a gap that benchmark designers and deploying organizations need to account for.

From CAMO's perspective on algorithmic foundations for trustworthy AI-driven decisions, this is a calibration problem with practical consequence: any organisation or researcher using LLM-simulated agents to pilot-test incentive schemes, mechanism designs, or market experiments should treat the outputs as category-level approximations, not behavioural ground truth. The gap between simulated cooperation and real end-game defection, for instance, would systematically mislead predictions about how employees or counterparties behave when stakes and horizons become concrete.
data.claude_summary: When LLMs are used as stand-ins for human participants in behavioural economics experiments, do they actually replicate human decision-making? This study tests that assumption across two classic games — a p-beauty contest and a public goods game — varying model scale, temperature, quantisation, and instruction-tuning across 360 conditions. The finding is that LLMs behave as fixed, scale-determined 'level-k' reasoners: larger models reason more steps ahead, but none update beliefs dynamically across rounds or backward-induct from a game's end. Human contributions to public goods decay over rounds; LLMs stay flat or rise. LLMs respond to horizon framing (indefinite vs finite) but ignore their actual position within that horizon, so no end-game defection appears. The implication is that LLMs simulate a cognitive category, not a cognitive process.
data.key_takeaway: LLMs mimic a fixed level of strategic reasoning set by model scale but do not update beliefs or backward-induct, making them unreliable substitutes for human participants in dynamic behavioural experiments.

data.centre_angle: This study provides one of the most methodologically careful estimates of enterprise AI adoption to date, anchoring measurement to legally accountable SEC disclosures rather than survey self-reporting or media mentions. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, the finding that only 11% of S&P 500 firms have achieved deep integration — despite near-universal executive interest — is consistent with what our Deloitte-HKU AI Adoption Index 2026 identifies as a paradox of promise and performance: adoption is widespread in rhetoric but shallow in practice, with organisational and executional barriers rather than technical ones doing most of the blocking. The J-curve in profitability, alongside the absence of a productivity signal, also invites caution about linear narratives of AI-driven firm-level gains, and suggests that the transition costs of deep integration are real and unevenly distributed.
data.claude_summary: How deeply has AI actually penetrated large U.S. enterprises, beyond the hype? Analysing SEC 10-K filings from 2016 to 2025 — where firms face legal penalties for misleading disclosures — the study finds that only 11% of S&P 500 companies had AI deeply integrated into their business processes by 2025, with another 10% using it in production or service delivery. Adoption has more than quadrupled since 2022, but remains heavily concentrated in the technology sector, which accounts for two-thirds of deep integration. Profitability follows a J-curve as firms move toward deep adoption, yet no measurable differences in capital expenditure or productivity have emerged. Among tech firms, larger companies and those with higher Tobin's q adopt more aggressively; among non-tech firms, no such pattern holds.
data.key_takeaway: Despite quadrupling since 2022, deep enterprise AI integration reaches only 11% of S&P 500 firms, and no productivity gains are yet visible in the data — suggesting the hard work of embedding AI into business processes is still largely ahead of most companies.

data.claude_summary: As large AI models have expanded in capability, their computational and energy costs have grown sharply. This survey maps the full landscape of techniques aimed at making large model development more sustainable: efficient architectural choices (including attention optimization and sparse models), training strategies that reduce data and parameter overhead, and hardware-software co-design approaches that cut energy use at the chip and infrastructure level. The authors also survey applications of these efficient models to sustainability-relevant domains such as remote sensing and national infrastructure. The paper frames green AI not as a single fix but as a stack of interlocking decisions spanning model design, training, deployment, and hardware — and calls for standardized benchmarks to measure progress.

data.centre_angle: This study shows that delegating market decisions to a shared algorithmic provider can produce coordinated outcomes that are empirically indistinguishable from cartel behaviour, even when the competing firms have no direct contact. From CAMO's perspective on algorithmic decision-making, the finding raises a structural question that extends well beyond electricity markets: when organisations outsource consequential decisions to the same AI or optimisation layer, standard competitive analysis becomes unreliable. The paper's conduct-test methodology — estimating counterfactual decisions from first principles and comparing them against observed behaviour — offers a template for regulators and managers who need to audit whether a shared algorithm is steering decisions toward individual or collective optima.
data.claude_summary: When competing firms use bidding algorithms supplied by the same third-party provider, their bids synchronise in ways that effectively coordinate market behaviour without explicit collusion. Studying five-minute battery bids in Australia's electricity market, the paper finds that batteries sharing an autobidding provider forgo profitable dispatch during evening peaks to protect the revenues of same-provider rivals. A conduct parameter near one indicates near-perfect coordination. The effect activates only when a provider controls more than roughly 30% of near-margin capacity, and the estimated consumer harm is $5.5 million annualised. Crucially, standard ownership-based concentration measures would miss this entirely, since the batteries belong to different firms.
data.key_takeaway: When rivals share the same algorithmic bidding provider, the algorithm can act as a de facto coordinator — with real consumer costs that ownership-based competition analysis is blind to.

data.centre_angle: This paper argues that cheaper AI is neither inherently good nor bad for formal employment in developing economies — the outcome is determined by the elasticity of substitution between AI capital and human labor, a parameter that varies by sector, task structure, and institutional context. From CAMO's perspective on how AI reshapes career paths and employment structures, this framing reinforces a point implicit in our research on job design: AI's labor-market effect is an organizational and contractual question as much as a technological one. The concern raised in our 'Toward a Bad Job Economy' working paper — that AI disproportionately lowers the cost of satisfactory rather than excellent performance — is compounded in developing-economy settings where informal employment already absorbs displaced formal workers, creating a structural floor beneath which wage pressure can accumulate silently.
data.claude_summary: When AI capital becomes cheaper, does it create formal jobs or push workers into informality? This paper builds a dynamic general equilibrium model calibrated to a developing economy with a large informal sector and finds that the answer hinges entirely on one parameter: whether AI substitutes for or complements formal workers. Under substitution, falling AI prices erode formal labor demand and expand the informal buffer. Under complementarity, they raise formal employment, wages, and output. The model is a small open economy with imported AI capital and country risk, so exchange-rate and financial conditions shape the magnitude of both effects. The core contribution is showing that the same price shock can produce diametrically opposite distributional outcomes depending on the structural relationship between AI and labor.
data.key_takeaway: Whether cheap AI creates or destroys formal jobs in developing economies depends on whether AI substitutes for or complements local workers — a policy distinction that matters more than the price of the technology itself.

matched_camo.reason: Both papers analyze how AI-driven cost reductions can restructure employment toward lower-quality or lower-wage arrangements rather than simply expanding output, with this paper extending that logic to the formal-informal labor divide in developing economies.

data.centre_angle: This paper argues that the systemic risk embedded in AI-driven finance stems not from algorithms per se but from their convergence on similar model architectures and input signals. From CAMO's perspective on the statistical and algorithmic foundations of trustworthy AI-driven decisions, this is a macro-scale demonstration of a general principle: when AI systems share training signals and decision rules, their errors do not diversify — they amplify. CAMO's work on self-fulfilling bias in online learning algorithms (see 'Dynamic Selection in Algorithmic Decision-making') shows an analogous mechanism at the firm level, where endogenous data feedback reinforces initial errors; this paper extends a related logic to systemic, cross-border financial instability.
data.claude_summary: When AI-driven fund managers rely on similar models and signals, their trading decisions become correlated — and that correlation amplifies capital outflows from emerging markets when U.S. monetary policy tightens. This paper builds a two-region macro-financial model and tests it against equity portfolio flow data from 19 emerging markets between 2000 and 2024. The key finding is that model homogeneity, not algorithmic speed or scale, is the destabilizing force: correlated errors compound during high-volatility periods, while diverse models allow errors to cancel out. The policy implication shifts attention away from limiting non-bank intermediation and toward preserving algorithmic diversity in asset management.
data.key_takeaway: AI-driven herding in asset management destabilizes emerging-market capital flows not because algorithms are fast, but because too many of them are thinking alike.

data.centre_angle: This study argues that scaling AI-generated contributions in open-source software outpaces the governance structures maintainers have to assess risk and assign accountability — a coordination failure distinct from purely technical concerns. From CAMO's perspective on AI adoption, the deeper implication is that AI deployment typically optimises task throughput while leaving the organisational infrastructure for oversight and accountability underdeveloped; real adoption risk sits in those gaps, not in the technology itself. data.claude_summary: As AI coding agents flood open-source repositories with machine-generated contributions, human maintainers face a governance bottleneck: they cannot assess risk, accountability, or evidence at the pace agents produce code. This paper diagnoses the problem through an audit of 50 GitHub repositories — finding fragmented AI-governance signals but no coherent framework — and proposes the Agent Governance Manifest (AGM), a repository-hosted contract linking contributor-side evidence preparation to maintainer-side verification authority. In controlled evaluations, AGM-supported reviewers correctly identified risk labels in 37 of 38 cases versus 15 of 37 without it, and reported substantially higher perceived review support. The study frames governability as a distinct layer above mere traceability, positioning the AGM as infrastructure for keeping human judgment authoritative in AI-mediated workflows.
data.key_takeaway: When AI agents generate contributions faster than humans can audit them, the critical investment is governance infrastructure that preserves human decision authority — not more agent capability.

data.centre_angle: This paper argues that the question of whether to automate a role should be governed by a structured protocol that prices systemic risks — tacit knowledge erosion, resilience reduction, regulatory exposure — which conventional ROI frameworks leave off the balance sheet. data.claude_summary: Standard automation ROI calculations systematically ignore four categories of risk that erode long-term organizational performance: tacit knowledge loss, reduced resilience, regulatory exposure, and degradation of socio-institutional capital. Applied to stylized internal roles, the protocol reverses automation decisions that standard cost-benefit analysis would approve. data.key_takeaway: Before automating any role, organizations need a structured protocol that prices tacit knowledge loss and resilience risk — costs that standard ROI calculations will not surface on their own.

data.centre_angle: This paper addresses a practical gap in AI governance: the absence of a systematic, auditable method for tracking whether a deployed AI system remains within acceptable trustworthiness bounds over time. From CAMO's perspective on algorithmic decision-making, the implication is significant — organizations deploying AI at scale need more than static validation at launch; they need continuous, documentable reassessment mechanisms that can withstand regulatory scrutiny. This work provides a formal scaffolding for exactly that, though its value to managers will depend on whether governance teams can operationalize interpretable rule-learning within their existing compliance workflows.
data.claude_summary: How do you know whether an AI system is still trustworthy six months after deployment — and how do you document that judgment in a way auditors can verify? This paper proposes a structured methodology: a formal framework that encodes trustworthiness as interpretable rules over measurable dimensions, and a governance procedure that embeds those rules into a lifecycle workflow covering design-time labeling, post-deployment monitoring, reassessment, and reporting. Using decision trees as the interpretable model class, the approach generates explicit trustworthiness plateaus and two diagnostics — boundary margins and profile drift — to flag when a system is approaching or has crossed a governance threshold. The methodology is positioned as an evidential support layer, not a replacement for legal or expert judgment.
data.key_takeaway: Organizations deploying AI need structured, auditable methods to document whether a system remains trustworthy after launch — not just at the point of initial approval.

data.centre_angle: This paper derives formal conditions under which AI substitutes for human labor across organizational layers, finding that middle management faces structural — not merely incidental — vulnerability, and that even highly skilled workers lose protection once AI capability crosses a threshold shaped by organizational depth. From CAMO's perspective on AI and jobs, the result complements our own work on job design: the 'bad job economy' paper (Toward a Bad Job Economy) shows a parallel mechanism whereby AI lowers the cost of satisfactory performance and induces firms to replace high-effort roles, and the HAT model here offers a complementary structural account of where those replacements concentrate in a hierarchy. Together, both lines of work suggest that the workforce risk from AI is not uniform across levels — it is shaped by organizational architecture, cost asymmetries, and incentive design simultaneously.
data.claude_summary: When does AI replace a human worker, and under what organizational conditions? This paper presents a formal model of Human-AI Task Allocation (HAT) in hierarchical organizations, deriving a precise 'substitution principle' based on the economic asymmetry between human skill acquisition (costly and slow) and AI capability scaling (cheaper and faster). The model predicts that AI adoption can produce abrupt workforce transitions rather than gradual ones, that middle-management roles face elevated vulnerability, and that highly skilled workers are protected only up to a threshold shaped by organizational depth and risk differentials. The analysis also suggests AI flattens hierarchies and widens managerial spans of control. The paper is a working paper from arXiv and has not yet undergone peer review.
data.key_takeaway: AI replacement in organizations is not random — it concentrates in middle management and follows a predictable structural logic tied to cost asymmetries, organizational depth, and risk, meaning firms can anticipate vulnerability hot-spots rather than react to them.
